# Introduction {#sec-chapter1}

Technical debt (TD) is not an abstract software quality concern. In mission-critical trading IT, it translates into delayed recovery, accumulating infrastructure risk and governance blind spots. The sections below establish why the absence of a quantitative, service-level measurement mechanism represents a specific and costly gap, and how this thesis addresses it.

## Background and Motivation

TD describes the implied future cost of accepting short-term technical compromises over more robust solutions [@cunninghamWyCashPortfolioManagement1992]. The concept has since expanded from source code quality to the architectural, design, test and documentation dimensions of complex IT systems [@kruchtenTechnicalDebtMetaphor2012]. Its operational and financial consequences are measurable and compound over a small number of years [@bankerTechnicalDebtFirm2020]. In trading environments they are intensified by continuous availability requirements, vendor-dominated architectures and regulatory oversight [@finmaCircular202312024], making the absence of a quantitative prioritisation mechanism particularly costly [@hakiDigitalNudgingTechnical2023; @ramasubbuControllingTechnicalDebt2021].

## Problem Statement

The TD literature lacks a standardised, quantitative framework for measuring and prioritising debt at the service level in vendor-dominated enterprise IT environments. In a review of 44 primary studies on prioritisation, @lenarduzziSystematicLiteratureReview2021 found that quantitative multi-criteria approaches are uncommon and that empirical validation on industrial datasets is rare. Much of this gap follows from where existing tools look. The dominant ones operationalise debt as the remediation effort implied by source code rule violations [@biazottoTechnicalDebtManagement2024], which makes them inapplicable where source code is unavailable, as is typical in trading IT. Even where code can be accessed, tools run against the same codebase return substantially divergent estimates [@amanatidisEvaluatingAgreementTechnical2020], and they leave infrastructure lifecycle debt, platform obsolescence and vulnerability debt largely unaddressed. Operational data offers a route around this, though the link is not yet demonstrated. DORA metrics, four delivery-performance measures from the DevOps Research and Assessment programme, are validated predictors of software delivery performance [@forsgrenAccelerate2018]. The step from degraded operational indicators to elevated TD severity has not been established empirically, so this study treats it as a testable proposition. None of the literature reviewed applied a multi-criteria decision-making framework to live service management data to produce a ranked TD prioritisation instrument for financial trading IT. This specific absence motivates the framework developed here.

## Research Aims and Objectives

This study develops a service-level quantitative framework for measuring and prioritising TD in mission-critical trading systems, grounded in operational service management data rather than source code analysis. Its objectives are as follows.

1. To review literature on TD measurement, prioritisation, financial enterprise IT governance and multi-criteria decision-making.
2. To identify and operationally define quantifiable TD indicators derived from live ITSM and CMDB records.
3. To design and apply a TOPSIS-based multi-criteria model for scoring and ranking services by TD priority.
4. To evaluate the framework analytically, by testing whether its rankings are stable under weight and temporal variation, reproduced by alternative methods, distinct from a single-criterion baseline and robust to the removal of individual services.

## Research Questions

The study is guided by the following primary research question.

> RQ1: *How can TD in mission-critical trading systems be prioritised quantitatively at the service level using operational data?*

Two secondary questions support the investigation.

- RQ2: To what extent do operational service management metrics serve as valid proxies for TD severity in vendor-dominated enterprise IT environments?
- RQ3: How stable are the resulting service rankings when criterion weights are perturbed?

Of these, RQ1 and RQ3 are design and robustness questions, answered by building the framework and examining how its rankings behave. RQ2 rests on a single empirical proposition, stated here so it can be weighed explicitly rather than assumed:

> Degraded operational service management metrics reflect accumulated TD rather than transient factors such as staffing, immature release practices or organisational disruption, and can therefore serve as valid proxies for TD severity.

The study treats this proposition as a conjecture to be evaluated against the evidence in @sec-chapter5, not as an established premise.

## Significance of the Study

The main academic contribution is a working prioritisation framework that did not previously exist for this environment, connecting operational service management with how TD is studied in software engineering. To the best of current knowledge, no prior study has applied TOPSIS to live operational records from a financial trading institution for TD prioritisation. Practically, the framework operates on data routinely available in enterprise ITSM and CMDB systems without requiring source code access, making it directly applicable to vendor-dominated trading IT architectures and supporting auditable remediation decisions in regulated environments.

The framework measures debt indirectly through operational proxies and expresses the result as a relative priority rather than an absolute quantity. The word "measuring" in the title carries that sense. It denotes a quantitative, reproducible ordering of services by debt priority, not a claim to have quantified the debt itself.

## Thesis Structure

@sec-chapter2 reviews the foundations across four bodies of literature and identifies the research gap. @sec-chapter3 describes the research design, methodology and ethical considerations. @sec-chapter4 presents the framework development and results, including data preparation and TOPSIS computation. @sec-chapter5 evaluates the framework against the criteria set in @sec-chapter3, covering stability, convergent and discriminant validity, rank reversal and weight-space robustness. @sec-chapter6 answers the research questions and gives a critical self-evaluation, the academic and practical contributions, and directions for future work.
